claims.text: The onset and progression of melting in FeNiCrCoCu nanoparticles is governed by preferential Cu segregation to the surface.
Cu has a lower melting point than Fe, Ni, Cr, and Co.
Cu has sufficiently low surface energy to favor its migration to the nanoparticle surface during heating.
Heating produces a Cu-enriched premelted layer at the nanoparticle surface.
The Cu-enriched surface layer is locally disordered.
The disordered surface layer propagates inward and accelerates melting relative to homogeneous melting.
The starting FeNiCrCoCu nanoparticles have a homogeneous elemental distribution and a well-defined crystalline structure.
Cu melting onset is approximately 800 K under the relevant nanoparticle heating conditions.
Sub-20 nm nanoparticles are small enough for surface effects to predominate.
A controlled heating rate can minimize thermal gradients and permit real-time imaging of the transition.
A Cu-enriched disordered surface layer lowers the local melting barrier.
Cu surface enrichment reduces local surface energy and destabilizes crystalline order.
Surface premelting triggers and accelerates complete melting by inward propagation of a liquid-like region.
Cu-enriched surface disorder and shape rounding will begin below the bulk melting point.
Complete melting will progress from the exterior toward the nanoparticle core.
In the absence of preferential surface segregation, melting would occur uniformly without a distinct Cu-enriched surface layer.
The proposed mechanism is expected to be observable in sub-20 nm nanoparticles under high vacuum.
Larger particle size or contaminants or coatings that inhibit atomic mobility may suppress the proposed mechanism.
